title: Granth and Panth
hook: scripture and community together carry the Guru

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Word as Guru: the shabad is the guru, and attention is the disciple. Your line was the word teaches. Did the line you carried speak into a real decision? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-six.

Stand at the back of a gurdwara hall and look forward. At the front, on a raised platform under a canopy, the Guru Granth Sahib, wrapped in cloth, someone sitting behind it waving a whisk. Now look down. Between you and the Granth, rows of people sitting on the floor: grandmothers, teenagers, a man still in his work uniform, a toddler wandering between laps. Two things fill that room. A book and a crowd. Yesterday we heard that the Guru is the Word. Today's lesson says the Word does not travel alone. In Sikh thought, the Guru is carried by both of the things in front of you.
screen: `AT THE FRONT: THE GRANTH.` → `ON THE FLOOR: THE PEOPLE.` → `A BOOK AND A CROWD.`

segments.voice: First, the two words. Granth means the book, the scripture: the Word you met yesterday, given a body of pages. Panth means the path, and by extension the people who walk it together, the Sikh community. Second, what tradition says happened. Sikh tradition remembers that Guru Gobind Singh named no human successor. Instead, tradition says, he passed the guruship to the Granth and to the Panth, the Khalsa community. Sikhs sum it up in a short phrase: Guru Granth, Guru Panth. The Guru as book. The Guru as people. Third, what the Granth says about the gathering. Guru Nanak asks a question in Sri Raag. In paraphrase: how is the true congregation known? And he answers: it is where the One Name is spoken. So the sangat isn't holy because of who's in it, or how important they are. It's holy because of what's spoken there. A crowd on a floor becomes a congregation when the Name is in the room. Fourth, why the two need each other. A book on a shelf with nobody reading it is silent. A crowd with nothing at the center can drift anywhere, toward whoever is loudest. Together, each keeps the other honest. The people read and sing the Granth, so the Word has a voice. The Granth holds the people to something older and steadier than any one of them. Tradition says that when Sikhs gather to decide serious matters, they do it in the Guru's presence, with the Granth in the room. Book and people.
screen: `GRANTH: THE BOOK. PANTH: THE PEOPLE.` · `GURU GRANTH, GURU PANTH.` · `WHERE THE NAME IS SPOKEN.` · `EACH KEEPS THE OTHER HONEST.` · then, large: `BOOK AND PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with the sangat. If you can get to a gurdwara this week, or any gathering where good words are spoken, go and sit on the floor for a while, and let the voices around you carry you. For right now, settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the people who have sat beside you in something good: a family table, a service, a hospital room, a circle of friends. See them one by one. Let the room fill up. Then breathe as if you were all breathing together. If you pray, you can let Waheguru be the word spoken in that room. The bell holds the time.
Granth and Panth. The scripture and the community, which together, Sikh tradition says, carry the Guru. Today's word.
Your line: book and people. Today, share one line of something good you've read with one person, so the words have a voice and the person has the words. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs gather as sangat in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib, and speak of the Guru as present in both the scripture and the Khalsa Panth, in the phrase Guru Granth, Guru Panth.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Granth is the Guru, and the community just follows it.
what it means: tradition says the Guru is carried by book and people together.
what a scholar hears: Guru Granth, Guru Panth; Guru Nanak in Sri Raag: the true congregation is where the One Name is spoken.

notes: Paraphrase of 'satsangat kaisee jaaneeai, jithai eko naam vakhaaneeai' (Sri Raag, Ang 72); please confirm the Ang and attribution to Guru Nanak.
The passing of guruship to Granth and Panth is presented as tradition; please confirm the framing and that naming the Panth as 'the Khalsa community' is acceptable.
The line that Sikhs gather to decide serious matters with the Granth in the room (gurmatta) is presented as tradition; please confirm or cut.
Glosses of granth as book and panth as path/community are standard usage, not built as etymology; please confirm.
